fixes.explanation: Close, but the verse says the enemies only hoped to overpower the Jews. Hoping is not winning, baker. I've hoped a cookie would cool itself the second it left the oven, and my mustache has the receipts. The text says their plan was overturned (Esther 9:1).
Not quite, friend. The text says the opposite: “No man could withstand them…” (Esther 9:2). Not plenty of men, not a few, not one. Nobody could hold their ground against them.
Right, it's false. The text says, “No man could withstand them, because the fear of them had fallen upon all peoples.” (Esther 9:2) Not one man could stand against them. Not ONE!

The verse doesn't give fleeing as the reason. It says the Jews assembled in their cities to attack those who sought to harm them. No one could withstand them because the fear of them had fallen upon all peoples (Esther 9:2).
Other way around, friend. The officials, satraps, governors and administrators helped the Jews (Esther 9:3). The text puts every one of them on the Jews' side.

Mordecai, Queen Esther's cousin (Esther 2:7), is the name. The verse says, “…because the fear of Mordecai had fallen upon them.” (Esther 9:3) The next verse adds that he exercised great power in the palace and his fame spread through the provinces (Esther 9:4). A name that travels that far, I can only dream about. My name spread as far as the end of one counter.

Esther is the queen, and she's right in the middle of this story. But this verse names a different person: the fear of Mordecai had fallen on the officials (Esther 9:3). Mordecai, her cousin (Esther 2:7), is the one with the great power in the palace (Esther 9:4).

Xerxes is the king, and these are his provinces (Esther 9:2). But the verse names someone else as the one whose fear had fallen on the officials: Mordecai (Esther 9:3). The next verse says his fame spread throughout the provinces (Esther 9:4). The king gets the crown, and Mordecai gets the fame.

True, and it's worth noticing. The text says the Jews killed Haman's ten sons, “…but they did not lay a hand on the plunder.” (Esther 9:10) Haman, son of Hammedatha, was the man who had plotted against the Jews (Esther 3:6). The king's letter had allowed plunder (Esther 8:11), and the text says they didn't take it.

That's the one. King Xerxes says, “Now what is your petition? It will be given to you.” (Esther 9:12) He asked her the same sort of thing before (Esther 5:6; 7:2). I like a king who keeps the door open. I spent years stuck in a junk drawer that never did.

The king doesn't ask about Mordecai here. His question to Queen Esther is about her request: “Now what is your petition?” (Esther 9:12) That's the same kind of question he asked her earlier (Esther 5:6; 7:2).

That's not what he asks. After telling her the count from Susa, he asks, “Now what is your petition? It will be given to you.” (Esther 9:12) He'd asked her about her petition before (Esther 5:6; 7:2). So his question is about what she wants, not why she came.
Tomorrow it is. Esther says, “…may the Jews in Susa also have tomorrow to carry out today’s edict…” (Esther 9:13). She asks for one more day, nothing longer.

Three hundred is the number. The text says the Jews in Susa came together again and “…put to death three hundred men there…” (Esther 9:15). I'll leave it just as the text gives it. The verse also says they didn't lay a hand on the plunder.
That's higher than the text says. On the fourteenth, the Jews in Susa put to death three hundred men (Esther 9:15). I want the number exactly right, so there it is.
That's lower than what the text says. The count for the fourteenth in Susa is three hundred men (Esther 9:15). I'd rather give you the number as written.

Right, the text says, “They killed 75,000 who hated them, but they did not lay a hand on the plunder.” (Esther 9:16) That's the count the text gives, and I'll let it stand. And again, the plunder stays untouched.
That's lower than the text says. The count in the royal provinces is 75,000 who hated them (Esther 9:16). I'd rather you get the real number.
That's higher than the text gives. In the royal provinces, the number is 75,000 (Esther 9:16). I'd rather keep it as written.
